name: Cannabis

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: Switches CB1 Gi coupling to Gs; implicated in addiction-related signalling

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Δ9-THC, as a partial CB1 agonist, inhibits adenylyl cyclase via Gαi/o (lower Emax than full agonists like JWH-018 or CP55,940), recruits β-arrestin-2 weakly, activates ERK1/2. CB1 partial agonism = ceiling on intoxication and key reason THC does not cause the seizures/AKI/MI seen with full synthetic agonists.

neuroimaging.finding: Acute Δ9-THC reduces [11C]OMAR (CB1 antagonist) binding by ~30% in cortex, confirming target engagement at recreational doses
Increased BOLD in striatum/ACC during reward and salience tasks; decreased in DLPFC during working memory

routes.notes: Smoking bioavailability 18-50% depending on smoking topography; terminal half-life is long (1-3 days) due to deep adipose redistribution.
First-pass metabolism produces ~equipotent 11-OH-THC, contributing to delayed/more intense effects of edibles.

concentration_effect.effect: psychomotor and cognitive impairment (critical tracking, stop signal, Tower of London)

metabolism.notes: 11-OH-THC is equipotent or slightly more potent at CB1 than parent; major active metabolite especially after oral dosing.
Inactive carboxylic acid; primary urinary marker (as glucuronide).

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C9*3/*3 carriers show ~3× higher THC AUC than *1/*1; clinically relevant for medical cannabis dosing.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Cortical CB1 receptors are downregulated in chronic daily cannabis smokers (~20% lower [18F]FMPEP-d2 binding, correlating with years of use) and return to normal levels after ~4 weeks of monitored abstinence (Hirvonen 2012).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 24-48h, peak 2-6 days, resolves 1-2 weeks. Irritability, anxiety, sleep disturbance with vivid dreams, decreased appetite, sweating.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Putative role in pain processing; clinical significance unclear
May contribute to metabolic effects and anti-inflammatory action
off_targets.notes: Citation removed: this value was attributed to doi:10.1111/j.1476-5381.2009.00467.x, which is the estrogenic activity of non-aromatic steroids. Verified against PubMed/Crossref in the 2026-08-01 topicality audit. The number is retained but is now unsourced — treat as unverified.

demographic_differences.sex: Women show 1.7× higher peak plasma Δ9-THC than men at same per-kg dose; possibly due to higher adipose redistribution.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly show slower clearance and greater sensitivity to cognitive/cardiovascular effects.
demographic_differences.weight: Higher BMI → larger Vd → longer detection window but delayed Cmax
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment significantly prolongs half-life; renal clearance minimal.

data_gaps_remaining: definitive Bmax data in human living brain for CB1 downregulation
notes: Δ9-THC's PARTIAL agonism at CB1 (~15-30% intrinsic activity vs CP55,940) is the single most important pharmacological fact distinguishing natural cannabis from synthetic cannabinoid full agonists. This ceiling effect is why THC has never produced confirmed lethal overdose: maximum CB1 activation is intrinsically limited regardless of dose.

name: Cannabichromene

binding.notes: Weak CB1 binding (~20× weaker than THC) — not the primary mechanism.
CB2 activity resides exclusively in (−) isomer; (+) isomer inactive at CB2.
Both enantiomers active at TRPA1 (stereo-non-selective).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Primary actions via TRP channel activation (TRPA1>>TRPV1) producing calcium influx; weak partial CB2 agonism contributes to anti-inflammatory effects.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Increases endogenous anandamide tone — may contribute to indirect endocannabinoid effects

data_gaps_remaining: in vivo TRPA1 contribution to subjective effects
notes: No clinical human PK data; classified as non-intoxicating because CB1 affinity is too weak for psychoactive effect at achievable doses.

name: Cannabidiolic acid

binding.notes: Bolognini 2013: CBDA is more potent than CBD at 5-HT1A in vitro and in vivo anti-nausea models.
Takeda 2008: CBDA IC50 ~2 µM at COX-2 with 9× selectivity over COX-1; methylation of carboxyl group abolishes selectivity — carboxylate is the pharmacophore.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 5-HT1A activation → Gi → decreased cAMP and neuronal hyperpolarisation (anti-nausea, anti-anxiety); COX-2 selective inhibition.

metabolism.notes: Decarboxylates to CBD on heating (smoking/vaping) or storage; in body, CBDA mostly stable but slowly converts.

notes: Raw cannabinoid acid in fresh plant material — converted to CBD by heat/UV/time. Mechanism differs from CBD: more potent 5-HT1A agonist, has selective COX-2 inhibition (CBD does not). Has been formulated as a metallic salt 'EPM301' for stability.

name: Cannabigerol

binding.notes: Cascio 2010: CBG is potent (sub-nM) α2-adrenoceptor agonist — likely dominant mechanism for in vivo effects (sedation, hypotension, anti-anxiety).
Cascio 2010: Moderate potency 5-HT1A antagonist; opposite direction from CBD.
Weak partial agonist / very weak antagonist.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: α2-adrenergic Gi signalling → decreased cAMP → reduced noradrenergic outflow (sedation, hypotension).

data_gaps_remaining: clinical CV monitoring data for high-dose CBG
notes: Often marketed as 'mother of all cannabinoids' (biosynthetic precursor). Importantly, primary pharmacology is NOT cannabinoid — sub-nM α2-adrenoceptor agonism is much more potent than CB1/CB2 activity. Safety concern: potential additive hypotension/bradycardia with clonidine or β-blockers.

name: CBDV

binding.notes: De Petrocellis 2011/2014: CBDV activates and rapidly desensitises TRPV1 — putative anticonvulsant mechanism.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: TRPV1/TRPA1 activation followed by Ca2+-dependent desensitisation reduces neuronal hyperexcitability — anticonvulsant in PTZ and audiogenic seizure models.

routes.notes: Generally well-tolerated; Phase 2 trial in drug-resistant focal epilepsy did NOT show efficacy (GW Pharma 2018).

notes: Propyl analogue of CBD. Studied as anticonvulsant (GWP42006), but Phase 2 trial in focal epilepsy was negative. Continues to be studied for autism (Rett, Fragile X).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Effectively no in vitro receptor pharmacology characterised; assumed pharmacologically silent like other carboxylic-acid cannabinoid precursors.

binding.notes: Aung et al 2000 founding measurement; ~4× more potent than Δ9-THC at CB1 AND full agonist (~100% efficacy vs THC's ~25%). This combination is what makes JWH-018 dramatically more dangerous than cannabis.

The paper states only qualitatively that JWH-018 has about 4x higher binding affinity than Delta-9-THC and an in vivo ED50 about 2x lower in mouse.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Rapid CB1 internalisation (hours); robust desensitisation within days. Heavy users develop severe physical dependence with prolonged withdrawal compared to cannabis.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset within 24 h, peak 2-7 d, can persist 2-4 weeks. Anxiety, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, tremor, GI distress, severe insomnia, craving. More severe than cannabis withdrawal.

class_name: Phytocannabinoids (mixed CB1 partial agonists, NAMs, and TRP modulators)
shared_mechanism: Plant-derived cannabinoids act through a constellation of targets: CB1/CB2 cannabinoid receptors (THC = partial agonist; CBN = weaker partial agonist; CBG/CBC = weak), GPCR allosterism (CBD = CB1 negative allosteric modulator), serotonergic (CBD = 5-HT1A agonist; CBDA = stronger 5-HT1A agonist; CBG = 5-HT1A antagonist), adrenergic (CBG = potent α2 agonist), TRP channels (CBC/CBD/CBDV/CBG → TRPV1/TRPV2/TRPA1 desensitisation), and enzyme inhibition (CBDA = COX-2; CBD = FAAH and major CYP isoforms). The CB1 partial agonism of THC (intrinsic activity ~15-30% vs full agonists) is the single pharmacological feature that prevents lethal overdose — there is a CEILING on receptor activation regardless of dose. Recent (Laprairie 2015) finding that CBD is a CB1 NAM means CBD reduces CB1-mediated effects of THC while having its own multi-target pharmacology.
shared_pk_summary: Highly lipophilic, large Vd (~10 L/kg), high protein binding (>95% albumin/lipoproteins). Smoked bioavailability 18-50%; oral 4-12% with marked food effect (3-5× fed:fasted). Hepatic metabolism by CYP2C9/CYP3A4/CYP2C19 with hydroxylation and glucuronidation. Active metabolite 11-OH-THC ≥ parent in potency (drives delayed/prolonged edible effects). CBD additionally inhibits CYP2C19 (potent) and CYP3A4 — clinically significant for clobazam, warfarin, mTOR inhibitors. Terminal half-lives are long (>24 h) due to deep adipose redistribution.
shared_safety: Natural cannabinoids: cannabis itself has not produced confirmed fatal overdose due to partial CB1 agonism. Major risks: tachycardia/dose-related anxiety/psychosis, cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome with chronic use, withdrawal (mild compared to synthetics). CBD-specific: hepatotoxicity (5-15% AST/ALT elevation in Epidiolex trials, doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1611618), drug interactions via CYP2C19/3A4. CBG-specific: hypotension/bradycardia from α2 agonism.
sar_summary: Pentyl side chain (C5) is optimal for CB1 binding — propyl analogues (THCV, CBDV) are weaker; heptyl (THCP) is dramatically more potent (Ki 1.2 nM vs 40 nM for THC). Carboxylated precursors (THCA, CBDA, CBGA) are pharmacologically distinct from decarboxylated forms — CBDA is more potent at 5-HT1A and selectively inhibits COX-2 due to the carboxylate. Δ8 vs Δ9 vs Δ10 isomers: Δ8 has ~2× weaker CB1 affinity than Δ9 but qualitatively similar pharmacology. Free phenolic OH at C-1 critical for CB1 binding.

shared_mechanism: SCRAs are typically FULL agonists at CB1 (intrinsic activity = 100% or 'super-Emax' >100% vs CP55,940) with affinities in the sub-nanomolar to low-nM range — 10-1000× more potent than Δ9-THC, which is a partial agonist (~25% efficacy). The combination of high affinity AND full intrinsic activity is the single most important toxicological fact: there is no receptor-level ceiling on activation, unlike THC. The dominant chemotypes are: (1) aminoalkylindoles (JWH-018, JWH-073, AM-2201) — early-generation; (2) indazole-3-carboxamides (AB/ADB/AMB/MDMB-PINACA/-BUTINACA/-FUBINACA series) — post-2014 ultrapotent; (3) indole-3-carboxamides (5F-MDMB-PICA, ADBICA); (4) adamantoylindoles (AM-1248, APICA); (5) cumyl/PINACA hybrids; (6) ester-linked quinolinyl indoles (PB-22, 5F-PB-22). Functional CB1 signalling: full Gαi/o → adenylyl cyclase inhibition; strong β-arrestin-2 recruitment correlates with seizure/cardiotoxicity. CB2 affinity is variable.
shared_pk_summary: Smoked or vaporised in herbal mixtures; controlled human PK essentially non-existent — only post-mortem and ER concentrations. Highly lipophilic, large Vd. Major metabolism: CYP3A4/CYP2C9/CYP1A2 hydroxylation (ω, ω-1, indole 6/7 positions); CES1 hydrolysis of methyl ester groups (5F-MDMB-PICA, 4F-MDMB-BINACA, AMB-FUBINACA) producing INACTIVE free carboxylic acids — short half-life of parent. Glucuronidation by UGT2B7/UGT1A3 produces urinary metabolites. Hydroxylated metabolites of aminoalkylindoles often retain CB1 affinity; some are neutral antagonists.
shared_safety: Severe and frequent: seizures (status epilepticus reported), acute kidney injury (especially XLR-11, MDMB-CHMICA, ADB-PINACA), myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, agitated delirium, severe vomiting, hyperthermia/rhabdomyolysis, acute psychosis, dependence/withdrawal more severe than cannabis. Mass-poisoning events: AMB-FUBINACA Brooklyn July 2016 (33 cases, NEJM); MDMB-CHMICA Europe 2014-2016 (29 deaths, 9 countries); ADB-PINACA Colorado 2013; MDMB-4en-PINACA multiple recent fatalities. Naloxone DOES NOT reverse — supportive care + benzodiazepines for agitation/seizures. Cannabinoid CB1 antagonists (rimonabant — withdrawn from clinical use; CB1 NAMs in development per Laprairie 2024 ITCM) are not clinically available as antidotes.
sar_summary: Aung 2000 SAR: minimum 3-carbon N-alkyl chain for CB1 affinity; pentyl (C5) optimal. ω-fluorination of pentyl (5F-) increases CB1 affinity AND metabolic stability vs parent. Substituting pentyl with cyclohexylmethyl (CHM) or 4-fluorobenzyl (FUB) maintains or enhances CB1 affinity. Head group SAR (Banister 2015-2021): tert-leucine (MDMB) > valine (AMB) > leucine (AB) > glycine for both potency and Emax. Indazole core often more potent than indole (PINACA > PICA). Ester linkages (PB-22, 5F-PB-22) give very high potency but rapid CES1 hydrolysis. Designer evasion 2019-: replacement of fluoropentyl with pent-4-enyl (MDMB-4en-PINACA), hexyl (ADB-HEXINACA), or 4-fluorobutyl (4F-MDMB-BINACA) to circumvent analogue laws.

class_name: Data integrity issues in source list
shared_mechanism: Three entries in the source list (4F-NEB, 4F-PHP, MADAM-6) are tagged 'synthetic-cannabinoid' but are NOT cannabinoids: 4F-PHP is a pyrrolidinophenone synthetic cathinone (stimulant, monoamine reuptake inhibitor); MADAM-6 is a Shulgin phenethylamine (6-methyl-MDMA, reported inactive); 4F-NEB does not match any known cannabinoid in the literature. The 'synthetic-cannabinoid' tags should be removed from the source data.
shared_pk_summary: Not applicable — these are not cannabinoids.
shared_safety: If users encounter these substances expecting cannabinoid-like effects (because the database labels them as such), they may misjudge dose and route. Especially dangerous for 4F-α-PHP (cathinone stimulant) — recreational doses are mg-range, not hundreds-of-mg.

binding.assay_notes: [3H]CP-55940, human cloned
binding.notes: Third independent Delta-9-THC CB1 figure, from the same Ray 2010 paper that anchors the psychedelic axis, so it shares a provenance frame with axis 1. That table lists three CB1 measurements — 13.7 nM (human cortical membranes), 15.3 nM (human cloned), 5.05 nM (human cloned, [3H]CP-55940) — and reports an average of 10.19 nM; CB2 average 16.85 nM. The 5.05 value is the single tightest human-cloned CP-55940-based measurement in that table.

binding.assay_notes: human CB1R, HEK-293T, BRET Gαi engagement (CB1R-Rluc / Gαi-mVenus), Emax read at 16 min
binding.notes: 36.1 ± 4.1% of CP55,940. Yano 2023 Table 1, CB1R-Gαi engagement at 16 min, Emax normalised against CP55,940 = 100% in the same assay. Reported as % of CP55,940 with SEM; pEC50 for THC could not be determined (ND), so this row carries efficacy only and no potency. The β-arrestin-2 arm of the same table gives a near-identical ordering (THC 36.0, AM2201 106.5, 5F-MDMB-PICA 147.7) and is deliberately NOT loaded: two pathway sets would partition into two ladders and the axis would pick one arbitrarily. This is the row the CB1 efficacy axis was missing: THC's three other comparable_sets are radioligand BINDING panels (Ki only, no Emax), so the ladder could not gate on any of them. MAGNITUDE rests on this one experiment; the ORDERING does not. Sachdev 2020 (doi:10.1002/prp2.566, HEK-CB1 CAMYEL, a different lab and a different assay) reports its group's prior quantitative work as "all SCRAs tested showed between 20- and 300-fold greater agonist activity at CB1 compared to THC", and describes THC as a partial agonist against high-efficacy SCRAs. That paper cannot substitute for this row — it reports no THC Emax at all (THC did not measurably stimulate its Gαs arm) — so treat 36.1% as one lab's figure for a fact many labs agree on in direction.

binding.notes: Same document as Delta-9 above, so the ~4.3x weaker CB1 binding of Delta-8 vs Delta-9 is an apples-to-apples statement. BUT other retrieved documents disagree on the size of that gap: 10.1016/j.ejmech.2024.116164 gives Delta-9 CB1 39 nM and Delta-8 CB1 40 nM (essentially IDENTICAL), and ChEMBL holds Delta-8 CB1 values spanning 28.5-78 nM across 8 documents. binding.notes: 9R epimer. Printed as EC50 101 nM (95% CI 81.9-125) and efficacy 64% (95% CI 62-66) relative to JWH-018. REFERENCE AGONIST IS JWH-018, NOT CP55,940 — this value cannot be dropped onto a CP55,940-normalized scale without a conversion the retrieved literature does not provide. Partial agonist.

binding.assay_notes: human CB1, recombinant CHO-K1, aequorin luminescence (G-protein pathway)
binding.notes: 9S epimer. Printed as EC50 1190 nM (95% CI 951-1490) and efficacy 68% (95% CI 65-71). THE KEY HHC FINDING: the epimers differ ~11.8x in POTENCY (101 vs 1190 nM) but are statistically INDISTINGUISHABLE in EFFICACY (64% vs 68%). So on an efficacy axis the two epimers sit on top of each other; the 9R/9S distinction belongs on a potency axis, not this one. Products contain variable mixtures — reported 9R:9S ratios range 0.2:1 to 2.4:1 in US retail product and 0.27-0.89 in Belgian seizures — so a given package's potency is genuinely unpredictable.

binding.notes: Same document as CBN/CBG. Retrieved CBD CB1 values scatter 151-4350 nM across five documents. The robust, source-independent statement is only the ORDER: CBD binds CB1 roughly two orders of magnitude more weakly than THC and is not meaningfully an orthosteric CB1 agonist. Efficacy null — no CB1 Emax retrieved, which is appropriate since CBD's pharmacology is not orthosteric CB1 agonism.
